screens.title: Cracking Wireless Encryption
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn the practical steps ethical hackers use to evaluate wireless encryption. We start by examining why WEP is fundamentally broken and how simple packet collection and replay attacks let tools deduce its key. Then we'll move to WPA and WPA2-PSK, where the target is not the running cipher but the four-way handshake: capturing that exchange enables offline password guessing. You will see concrete, repeatable command sequences using the Aircrack-ng suite, learn how to force a handshake with deauthentication, and how to run offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake. Throughout, I’ll emphasize common mistakes you will encounter in the field — for example, failing to collect enough IVs for WEP, or not confirming a complete WPA handshake — and the right checks to perform. Importantly, every technique will be framed by safety and legality: do this only in a controlled lab or with explicit permission. By the end of the chapter you should be able to run a controlled capture and attempt a crack in a lab environment, explain why a strong pre-shared key resists dictionary attacks, and recommend mitigations to secure wireless networks.

screens.title: Why WEP is broken
screens.narratorSegment: WEP’s failure begins with a small initialization vector and a vulnerable composition of IV and key material. The IV is a short value that is combined with the secret key to produce a keystream. Because the IV is small, it repeats often. Reuse of the same IV with the same key produces repeated keystream fragments. An attacker who collects many packets with different IVs can apply statistical analysis to recover the underlying key. In practice this means that passive capture alone, or simple packet injection to stimulate traffic, yields the tens of thousands of IV samples needed for key recovery. A concrete example is capturing ARP packets: ARP traffic is predictable and small, so when re-encrypted with different IVs it produces many usable ciphertexts with the same plaintext structure. A common misconception is to assume WEP fails because of a weak cipher alone — the real issue is the combination of a non-unique IV and reuse with the same key. The core takeaway is that protocol design choices at the IV level can make a cipher practically useless, and that is exactly what happened with WEP.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: WEP's tiny IV space and IV reuse enable statistical attacks that recover the key after enough ciphertext is collected.

content.html:
Core Concept
Why WEP is broken
A short IV and IV reuse make the cipher vulnerable to statistical key recovery.
Definition
The Initialization Vector is a small, non-secret value combined with the key; in WEP its limited range causes reuse and repeated keystream fragments.
Analogy
Like reusing a one-time pad many times: repeat usage leaks patterns that let an attacker deduce the key.
Concrete example
Capturing many ARP packets yields repeated plaintext structure; with IVs you can correlate ciphertexts and recover the WEP key statistically.
Key points
  • WEP uses a short IV which frequently repeats in real traffic.
  • IV reuse produces repeated keystream fragments that leak key material.
  • Active injection (ARP replay) speeds IV collection to reach statistical thresholds.
Key Takeaway

Protocol parameters such as IV length matter. A strong cipher can be broken by poor IV design.

screens.title: WEP cracking workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A WEP attack is a sequence of repeatable steps. First, you prepare your adapter by enabling monitor mode so it can capture raw 802.11 frames. Next, run airodump-ng focused on the target AP to collect packets and the IVs shown in the capture output. The critical step is forcing or encouraging traffic that produces many IVs; this is where the ARP replay attack comes in: capture a valid ARP request and re-inject it repeatedly so the AP re-encrypts and emits new IVs. When the #Data or IV counts grow into the tens of thousands, run aircrack-ng on the capture file and let it apply statistical techniques to deduce the key. Each step has checks: confirm monitor mode created a new interface, confirm airodump-ng shows the target BSSID and rising #Data, and ensure your injection tool reports successful packet injection. A common troubleshooting step is to confirm an associated client exists; without an associated client you may need to use fake authentication to get one. Performing these steps in order helps isolate failures and makes the cracking attempt reproducible in a lab.

keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Monitor mode → targeted capture → stimulate IVs (ARP replay) → collect enough IVs → run aircrack-ng.

content.html:
Process Flow
WEP cracking workflow
1
Start monitor mode
Enable raw frame capture and note the monitor interface name. This is the foundation for all subsequent steps.
2
Capture IVs with airodump-ng
Focus on the target BSSID and channel, and save packets to a capture file for later analysis.
3
Stimulate traffic (ARP replay)
Re-inject captured ARP packets to force the AP to emit many IVs quickly.
4
Run aircrack-ng
When IVs are sufficient, run the cracker on the capture file to deduce the WEP key.
Command examples (visual)
sudo airmon-ng start wlan0
sudo airodump-ng --bssid <TARGET_AP_BSSID> -c <CHANNEL> -w wep_capture wlan0mon
sudo aireplay-ng --arpreplay -b <TARGET_AP_BSSID> -h <CLIENT_MAC> wlan0mon
sudo aircrack-ng wep_capture-01.cap
Check airodump-ng output for #Data growth. If it stalls, confirm injection success or authenticated client presence.

screens.title: ARP Replay attack
screens.narratorSegment: The ARP replay attack is the practical accelerator for WEP cracking. ARP is a small, frequently-used protocol with predictable packet content, which makes it ideal for repeated re-encryption. The technique begins by capturing a legitimate ARP request from the network. That captured request is replayed — injected back into the wireless medium — so the access point treats it as a new outgoing packet and encrypts it again with a new IV. Each re-encryption yields a new IV and ciphertext pair the attacker can collect. Over repeated injections you quickly gather tens of thousands of IVs, which is often enough for aircrack-ng’s statistical methods to recover the key. If no client is associated with the AP you can authenticate your testing adapter to the AP (a fake authentication) to become an associated client and then inject ARP requests from your station. A common misconception is that ARP replay requires user interaction; in reality, once you have a capture and can inject packets, the attack is highly automated and repeatable in a lab. Remember to stop injection if you do not have permission to avoid disrupting users.

keyIdea.title: Why ARP replay works
keyIdea.text: ARP packets provide repeatable plaintext structure; re-injecting them forces new IVs and accelerates IV collection for WEP cracking.

content.html:
Process Flow
ARP Replay attack
Capture a valid ARP request and inject it repeatedly to force the AP to emit many IVs.
Step-by-step
  1. Capture a live ARP request with airodump-ng.
  2. Use aireplay-ng to re-inject the captured ARP packet repeatedly.
  3. Monitor #Data in airodump-ng until IV counts are high enough.
Fake authentication
If no client exists, perform a fake authentication to associate your adapter, then inject ARP packets.
Command callouts
sudo airodump-ng --bssid <TARGET_AP_BSSID> -c <CHANNEL> -w wep_capture wlan0mon
# capture an ARP request then
sudo aireplay-ng --arpreplay -b <TARGET_AP_BSSID> -h <CLIENT_MAC> wlan0mon
# OR fake authenticate then inject
sudo aireplay-ng -1 0 -a <TARGET_AP_BSSID> -h <YOUR_MAC> wlan0mon
sudo aireplay-ng -3 -b <TARGET_AP_BSSID> -h <YOUR_MAC> wlan0mon
Watch for injection success messages and rising IV counts. Stop immediately if testing outside a permitted lab.

screens.title: Capturing IVs and cracking WEP
screens.narratorSegment: Collecting IVs is the measurement that determines success for WEP cracking. Tools will show a #Data column that reflects how many useful encrypted packets were captured. In practice you often need tens of thousands of IVs for a reliable statistical recovery. Using ARP replay accelerates this accumulation. When you decide to attempt the crack, run aircrack-ng on the saved capture file; the tool applies statistical attacks against the collected IVs and prints a recovered key if successful. An example workflow is running airodump-ng with capture saving enabled and watching the file update as packets arrive. If aircrack-ng fails, check whether you had enough IVs, whether the capture contains many identical frames, or whether injection actually worked. A common mistake is to run the cracker too soon; another is to assume any capture file is suitable. Confirm the #Data value and visually inspect the capture size. In a lab, you can repeat injection and capture until the thresholds are met, then re-run the cracker. Capturing IVs and cracking WEP means tens of thousands of ivs are typically needed; confirm #data growth before launching the statistical crack.. In practical terms, how much data you need and running aircrack-ng. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Capturing IVs and cracking WEP
Measure #Data and IVs, then run aircrack-ng when thresholds are met.
Checkpoints
  • Confirm the capture file is growing and shows the target BSSID.
  • Watch the #Data column; tens of thousands of IVs are commonly required.
  • Only run aircrack-ng once IV accumulation is sufficient.
Example command
sudo aircrack-ng wep_capture-01.cap
# aircrack-ng will display progress and, on success, the recovered WEP key
If cracking fails, re-check IV counts, confirm injection, and re-run capture until thresholds are reached. Patience and correct measurement are the keys.

screens.title: WPA/WPA2-PSK fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: WPA and WPA2-PSK use a structured handshake to derive session keys from a pre-shared key. The four-way handshake exchanges nonces and verification data so the client and access point can derive a Pairwise Master Key, then a Pairwise Transient Key for encryption. The handshake itself does not reveal the PSK directly, but it contains cryptographic material that lets an attacker verify guesses offline. That is the essential contrast with WEP: instead of exploiting IV reuse, the attacker captures the handshake and then tests candidate passwords by deriving the same cryptographic values and comparing them to the captured exchange. A concrete example: capture the handshake between a client and AP, then run a wordlist through aircrack-ng; the tool derives keys from each candidate and checks them against the handshake records. A common misconception is to think capturing the handshake automatically reveals the key; it does not. Success depends on the PSK being present in the wordlist and having sufficient entropy, which is why long, random PSKs are effective defenses. WPA/WPA2-PSK fundamentals means the four-way handshake authenticates client and ap and derives session keys; capturing it enables offline verification of psk guesses.. In practical terms, four-way handshake and why offline attacks work. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
WPA/WPA2-PSK fundamentals
The four-way handshake exchanges nonces and authentication data to derive session keys; a captured handshake enables offline PSK verification.
Concrete example
Capture the four-way handshake when a client connects or reconnects. With that capture, an attacker can test candidate passwords offline against the recorded material.
Misconceptions
  • Capturing a handshake does not immediately reveal the PSK.
  • Offline attacks only succeed if the PSK is in the wordlist or guess set.
  • A long, random PSK resists practical dictionary attacks.
Key Takeaway

WPA2 shifts the attacker’s task from intercepting weak IVs to finding the PSK; strong PSKs stop offline attacks.

screens.title: Capturing the four-way handshake
screens.narratorSegment: Capturing a valid four-way handshake requires recording the exchange when a client authenticates or re-authenticates with the AP. Start by putting the adapter into monitor mode and running airodump-ng targeted at the AP’s BSSID and channel while saving output to a file. If a client is already associated, you can force a reconnect using a deauthentication attack, which causes the client to re-authenticate and perform the handshake. In a lab, run a limited number of deauth packets to avoid excessive disruption. Watch airodump-ng for the 'WPA Handshake: ' indicator which confirms a complete handshake was observed. If the indicator does not appear, either the client did not complete the exchange or packets were missed. A common troubleshooting step is to increase monitor sensitivity, confirm channel locking, or try deauthenticating a different client. Always verify the capture file and only proceed to offline cracking when the handshake is present and complete. Capturing the four-way handshake means confirm airodump-ng shows 'wpa handshake' for the target ap before attempting offline attacks.. In practical terms, using airodump-ng and forcing reconnects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Confirm airodump-ng shows 'WPA Handshake' for the target AP before attempting offline attacks.

content.html:
Core Concept
Capturing the four-way handshake
Run airodump-ng with the target BSSID and channel, and save the capture. Force a reconnect if needed via deauthentication.
Command sequence (visual)
sudo airodump-ng --bssid <TARGET_AP_BSSID> -c <CHANNEL> -w wpa_capture wlan0mon
# in a new terminal to force reconnect
sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 5 -a <TARGET_AP_BSSID> -c <CLIENT_MAC> wlan0mon
Checks & troubleshooting
  • Confirm monitor interface and channel lock.
  • Verify airodump-ng shows the target BSSID and clients.
  • Look for the explicit 'WPA Handshake' indicator to ensure completeness.
Ethical note: Deauthentication disconnects users. Use minimal packets and always have permission to test.

screens.title: Deauthentication attack
screens.narratorSegment: A deauthentication attack sends frames that cause a client to drop its connection to an access point, often triggering a reconnect that performs the four-way handshake. In practice, you run a deauth command targeting a specific client or the AP as a whole. For lab use, send a small number of deauth frames to avoid prolonged disruption; for aggressive capture you might use continuous deauth, but only in a permitted environment. Observe the client behavior and watch for the handshake indicator in your capture tool. If no client reconnects, try targeting another associated client or wait for a natural reconnection. Misuse of deauthentication frames is disruptive and can break services; a common error is leaving continuous deauth running inadvertently. Always stop injection as soon as you confirm the handshake. In short, deauthentication is a practical capture tactic but must be balanced with ethical constraints and minimal disruption. Deauthentication attack means use deauthentication sparingly in a lab to force a handshake; avoid continuous disruptive attacks on production networks.. In practical terms, forcing clients to reconnect (with ethics and limits). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: A deauthentication attack sends frames that cause a client to drop its connection to an access point, often triggering a reconnect that performs the four-way handshake. In practice, you run a deauth command targeting a specific client or the AP as a whole. For lab use, send a small number of deauth frames to avoid prolonged disruption; for aggressive capture you might use continuous deauth, but only in a permitted environment. Observe the client behavior and watch for the handshake indicator in your capture tool. If no client reconnects, try targeting another associated client or wait for a natural reconnection. Misuse of deauthentication frames is disruptive and can break services; a common error is leaving continuous deauth running inadvertently. Always stop injection as soon as you confirm the handshake. In short, deauthentication is a practical capture tactic but must be balanced with ethical constraints and minimal disruption. Deauthentication attack means use deauthentication sparingly in a lab to force a handshake; avoid continuous disruptive attacks on production networks.. In practical terms, forcing clients to reconnect (with ethics and limits). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ethical deauth
keyIdea.text: Use deauthentication sparingly in a lab to force a handshake; avoid continuous disruptive attacks on production networks.

content.html:
Process Flow
Deauthentication attack
Send targeted deauth frames to force a client to reconnect and trigger the four-way handshake.
Command example
sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 5 -a <TARGET_AP_BSSID> -c <TARGET_CLIENT_MAC> wlan0mon
# Or deauth all clients
sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 5 -a <TARGET_AP_BSSID> wlan0mon
Guidelines & mistakes
  • Use a small number of deauth frames in a lab to minimize disruption.
  • Confirm handshake capture quickly and stop injection immediately.
  • Do not run deauth on networks without permission; it is disruptive.
Warning

Continuous deauth can cause service outage. Only use in controlled tests.

screens.title: Offline dictionary attack
screens.narratorSegment: Once you have a captured four-way handshake, the offline attack is straightforward: you load a wordlist and let the cracker derive and compare keys against the recorded handshake until a match is found or the wordlist is exhausted. The quality and coverage of your wordlist determine your chance of success: short or common passwords are often quickly found, while long random PSKs are effectively immune to dictionary attacks. A practical example is using a commonly available wordlist that contains known weak passwords used in lab setups, then running aircrack-ng pointing to the capture file and the wordlist. The attacker’s environment matters: C P U and G P U acceleration increase the rate at which candidates are tested. A common misconception is that a large wordlist guarantees success; it only helps if the PSK is included. For defenders, this demonstrates the importance of PSK entropy: a password manager or long random passphrase prevents these offline checks from succeeding in reasonable time. Offline dictionary attack means a captured handshake allows unlimited offline guessing; success depends solely on whether the psk is in the guess list.. In practical terms, using aircrack-ng with a wordlist against a captured handshake. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Offline dictionary attack
Run aircrack-ng with a wordlist against the captured handshake file to test candidate PSKs offline.
Example command
sudo aircrack-ng -w /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt wpa_capture-01.cap

screens.title: WEP vs WPA/WPA2-PSK
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing WEP and WPA/WPA2-PSK shows a clear evolution in attack surface. WEP is broken by design: its IV handling and key reuse allow statistical, practical attacks that recover the key after enough captured ciphertext. Attacking WEP is often a matter of capture and replay. WPA/WPA2-PSK, by contrast, resists this vector: its security rests on the entropy of the pre-shared key and a robust handshake. The attacker’s task shifts from clever protocol exploitation to offline password guessing. Practically, a weak PSK can be cracked quickly, but a strong, random PSK makes dictionary attacks infeasible. A common mistake is treating the two as equally easy targets; in reality, WEP is fast to exploit, while WPA2 requires accessible client interactions and a susceptible PSK. For defenders, the lesson is that protocol upgrades plus strong password policies are the right combination: replace WEP entirely and enforce high-entropy PSKs or enterprise authentication where possible. WEP vs WPA/WPA2-PSK means wep fails due to protocol design; wpa/wpa2-psk relies on key entropy and is only vulnerable when the psk is weak.. In practical terms, contrast the attack surface and practical difficulty. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

WEP vs WPA/WPA2-PSK
WEP
Attacked via IV collection and ARP replay. Low difficulty in a lab due to design flaws.

Capture and crack WPA2-PSK
Use a controlled AP with a known weak PSK and a connected client to practice the full workflow safely.
Starter commands
sudo airmon-ng start wlan0
sudo airodump-ng --bssid <TARGET_AP_BSSID> -c <CHANNEL> -w wpa_handshake_capture wlan0mon

screens.title: Common mistakes and mitigation
screens.narratorSegment: Many failed crack attempts are the result of avoidable mistakes. For WEP, the most frequent error is not collecting enough IVs or injecting packets to stimulate traffic. Check #Data, confirm injection success messages, and ensure an associated client exists or fake-authenticate to create one. For WPA/WPA2, missing or incomplete handshakes are the leading cause. Always verify the handshake indicator in your capture tool before attempting an offline crack. Another common misstep is relying on weak or inappropriate wordlists; use targeted custom lists for lab tests and comprehensive lists only when warranted. On the defensive side, mitigation is clear: deprecate WEP entirely; require strong PSKs, long passphrases, or better yet, enterprise authentication with per-user credentials. Educate users about password hygiene since WPA2-PSK security is only as good as the chosen passphrase. When reporting findings, document capture validation steps so stakeholders understand whether a failed crack was due to capture limitations or actual password strength. content.html:
Best Practices
Common mistakes and mitigation
Troubleshoot captures first; harden networks with protocol upgrades and strong keys.
Troubleshooting checklist
  • WEP: confirm high IV counts and injection success.
  • WPA2: confirm the complete WPA handshake in the capture.
  • Wordlists: use appropriate lists; weak lists lead to false negatives about key strength.
Hardening recommendations
  • Remove WEP from service; it is insecure by design.
  • Use long, random PSKs or enterprise authentication to prevent dictionary attacks.
  • Include capture validation in test reports so results are reproducible.
Key Takeaway

Most failed attacks are capture problems or strong keys. Document and validate every capture before claiming a network is secure or insecure.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn the practical steps ethical hackers use to evaluate wireless encryption. We start by examining why WEP is fundamentally broken and how simple packet collection and replay attacks let tools deduce its key. Then we'll move to WPA and WPA2-PSK, where the target is not the running cipher but the four-way handshake: capturing that exchange enables offline password guessing. You will see concrete, repeatable command sequences using the Aircrack-ng suite, learn how to force a handshake with deauthentication, and how to run offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake. Throughout, I’ll emphasize common mistakes you will encounter in the field — for example, failing to collect enough IVs for WEP, or not confirming a complete WPA handshake — and the right checks to perform. Importantly, every technique will be framed by safety and legality: do this only in a controlled lab or with explicit permission. By the end of the chapter you should be able to run a controlled capture and attempt a crack in a lab environment, explain why a strong pre-shared key resists dictionary attacks, and recommend mitigations to secure wireless networks.

By the end of these exercises you will be able to explain why WEP is vulnerable, execute an end-to-end WEP cracking workflow using Aircrack-ng, and describe the purpose of the WPA/WPA2 four-way handshake. Practically, you will put a compatible wireless adapter into monitor mode, capture the packets you need, force traffic or a handshake where appropriate, and run an offline crack or dictionary check. Each objective emphasizes safe lab practice: only run deauthentication or packet injection in environments where you have permission. You will also learn to diagnose common failures, such as insufficient IVs for WEP or an incomplete captured handshake for WPA2. Understanding these failure modes is important because it tells you whether the problem is a capture issue, a tooling issue, or simply that the target key is strong. Finally, you'll practice choosing and tuning a wordlist for offline attacks and recommend mitigations for defenders. This blend of explanation and hands-on steps will make you confident to reproduce captures and explain their security implications to stakeholders.

This second objectives slide focuses on safety, diagnostics, and interpretation. You will learn a lab checklist to ensure captures are valid: confirm monitor mode, note target BSSID and channel, record client MACs, and verify capture file sizes. You will learn ethical constraints: do not run deauthentication or packet injection on networks without permission, and always prefer a controlled lab AP and client. The slide also defines measurable diagnostic checks: for WEP, monitor the #Data and IV accumulation; for WPA2, confirm the 'WPA Handshake' indicator in airodump-ng. Finally, you will learn to interpret failures — small capture files usually mean no associated client or failed injection; failing to crack a WPA2 handshake with a large wordlist usually means the PSK is not present in that list. These practical rules shorten troubleshooting time and help you give accurate security advice after a test.

WEP’s failure begins with a small initialization vector and a vulnerable composition of IV and key material. The IV is a short value that is combined with the secret key to produce a keystream. Because the IV is small, it repeats often. Reuse of the same IV with the same key produces repeated keystream fragments. An attacker who collects many packets with different IVs can apply statistical analysis to recover the underlying key. In practice this means that passive capture alone, or simple packet injection to stimulate traffic, yields the tens of thousands of IV samples needed for key recovery. A concrete example is capturing ARP packets: ARP traffic is predictable and small, so when re-encrypted with different IVs it produces many usable ciphertexts with the same plaintext structure. A common misconception is to assume WEP fails because of a weak cipher alone — the real issue is the combination of a non-unique IV and reuse with the same key. The core takeaway is that protocol design choices at the IV level can make a cipher practically useless, and that is exactly what happened with WEP.

A WEP attack is a sequence of repeatable steps. First, you prepare your adapter by enabling monitor mode so it can capture raw 802.11 frames. Next, run airodump-ng focused on the target AP to collect packets and the IVs shown in the capture output. The critical step is forcing or encouraging traffic that produces many IVs; this is where the ARP replay attack comes in: capture a valid ARP request and re-inject it repeatedly so the AP re-encrypts and emits new IVs. When the #Data or IV counts grow into the tens of thousands, run aircrack-ng on the capture file and let it apply statistical techniques to deduce the key. Each step has checks: confirm monitor mode created a new interface, confirm airodump-ng shows the target BSSID and rising #Data, and ensure your injection tool reports successful packet injection. A common troubleshooting step is to confirm an associated client exists; without an associated client you may need to use fake authentication to get one. Performing these steps in order helps isolate failures and makes the cracking attempt reproducible in a lab.

The ARP replay attack is the practical accelerator for WEP cracking. ARP is a small, frequently-used protocol with predictable packet content, which makes it ideal for repeated re-encryption. The technique begins by capturing a legitimate ARP request from the network. That captured request is replayed — injected back into the wireless medium — so the access point treats it as a new outgoing packet and encrypts it again with a new IV. Each re-encryption yields a new IV and ciphertext pair the attacker can collect. Over repeated injections you quickly gather tens of thousands of IVs, which is often enough for aircrack-ng’s statistical methods to recover the key. If no client is associated with the AP you can authenticate your testing adapter to the AP (a fake authentication) to become an associated client and then inject ARP requests from your station. A common misconception is that ARP replay requires user interaction; in reality, once you have a capture and can inject packets, the attack is highly automated and repeatable in a lab. Remember to stop injection if you do not have permission to avoid disrupting users.

Collecting IVs is the measurement that determines success for WEP cracking. Tools will show a #Data column that reflects how many useful encrypted packets were captured. In practice you often need tens of thousands of IVs for a reliable statistical recovery. Using ARP replay accelerates this accumulation. When you decide to attempt the crack, run aircrack-ng on the saved capture file; the tool applies statistical attacks against the collected IVs and prints a recovered key if successful. An example workflow is running airodump-ng with capture saving enabled and watching the file update as packets arrive. If aircrack-ng fails, check whether you had enough IVs, whether the capture contains many identical frames, or whether injection actually worked. A common mistake is to run the cracker too soon; another is to assume any capture file is suitable. Confirm the #Data value and visually inspect the capture size. In a lab, you can repeat injection and capture until the thresholds are met, then re-run the cracker. Capturing IVs and cracking WEP means tens of thousands of ivs are typically needed; confirm #data growth before launching the statistical crack.. In practical terms, how much data you need and running aircrack-ng. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

WPA and WPA2-PSK use a structured handshake to derive session keys from a pre-shared key. The four-way handshake exchanges nonces and verification data so the client and access point can derive a Pairwise Master Key, then a Pairwise Transient Key for encryption. The handshake itself does not reveal the PSK directly, but it contains cryptographic material that lets an attacker verify guesses offline. That is the essential contrast with WEP: instead of exploiting IV reuse, the attacker captures the handshake and then tests candidate passwords by deriving the same cryptographic values and comparing them to the captured exchange. A concrete example: capture the handshake between a client and AP, then run a wordlist through aircrack-ng; the tool derives keys from each candidate and checks them against the handshake records. A common misconception is to think capturing the handshake automatically reveals the key; it does not. Success depends on the PSK being present in the wordlist and having sufficient entropy, which is why long, random PSKs are effective defenses. WPA/WPA2-PSK fundamentals means the four-way handshake authenticates client and ap and derives session keys; capturing it enables offline verification of psk guesses.. In practical terms, four-way handshake and why offline attacks work. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Capturing a valid four-way handshake requires recording the exchange when a client authenticates or re-authenticates with the AP. Start by putting the adapter into monitor mode and running airodump-ng targeted at the AP’s BSSID and channel while saving output to a file. If a client is already associated, you can force a reconnect using a deauthentication attack, which causes the client to re-authenticate and perform the handshake. In a lab, run a limited number of deauth packets to avoid excessive disruption. Watch airodump-ng for the 'WPA Handshake: ' indicator which confirms a complete handshake was observed. If the indicator does not appear, either the client did not complete the exchange or packets were missed. Comparing WEP and WPA/WPA2-PSK shows a clear evolution in attack surface. WEP is broken by design: its IV handling and key reuse allow statistical, practical attacks that recover the key after enough captured ciphertext. Attacking WEP is often a matter of capture and replay. WPA/WPA2-PSK, by contrast, resists this vector: its security rests on the entropy of the pre-shared key and a robust handshake. The attacker’s task shifts from clever protocol exploitation to offline password guessing. Practically, a weak PSK can be cracked quickly, but a strong, random PSK makes dictionary attacks infeasible. A common mistake is treating the two as equally easy targets; in reality, WEP is fast to exploit, while WPA2 requires accessible client interactions and a susceptible PSK. For defenders, the lesson is that protocol upgrades plus strong password policies are the right combination: replace WEP entirely and enforce high-entropy PSKs or enterprise authentication where possible.
